name: lifelines
why: A text-based genealogy program with an old-school ncurses feel and its own GEDCOM-driven world, worth an afternoon of wandering.

brief.what_it_is: LifeLines is a text-based genealogy program that runs in a terminal. Its main interactive program, llines, is a curses-style interface. Family data is stored in its own database format, and you typically get data in by importing a GEDCOM file exported from other genealogy software. Output comes from report scripts that produce things like ahnentafels, ancestor and descendant reports, groff and LaTeX books, and PostScript charts. The companion llexec runs reports non-interactively.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the real power of LifeLines is its scripting ability, and the reports it ships are the main draw. Tom Wetmore wrote it circa 1991-1994 as a GEDCOM-driven genealogy tool. He has since released it under an MIT-style license and no longer works on it.
brief.how_it_works: Data lives in LifeLines' own B-tree style database, which is why the kit includes btedit and dbverify for repair and checking. Users bring data in as GEDCOM, and report scripts are run against the database to produce text, groff, LaTeX, or PostScript output. The README does not describe the internals beyond this.

brief.install_notes: Dependencies: ncursesw or any curses with wide-character support. Native language support needs gettext and iconv, and is on by default; use --disable-nls to turn it off. Building from the git repo needs automake, autoconf, and bison 2.7+ or 3.1+. The test suite needs expect and bash. Documentation rebuilds need --with-docs plus xmlto, dblatex, lynx or links, and TeX packages. Windows users should use the binary distribution's Install.LifeLines.Windows.txt, or cygwin, or the MSVC6 project files. Debian, FreeBSD, and fink packages exist. The README also says the FreeBSD port lives at misc/lifelines.
brief.standout: It is a 1990s-era genealogy program that is still maintained, with a scripting report system that builds print-quality output such as LaTeX books and PostScript charts. It runs entirely in the terminal on curses.
brief.status: Maintained by the open-source community according to the source README, which describes version 3.2.0. The homepage points to 3.1.1 and 3.0.62 manuals. I did not find a release date or last commit date, so recency is not confirmed. The author has stepped away from the project.
brief.caveats: The README says the original website is dead and the old FTP repository no longer works. The X-based GUI is listed as future work, with a volunteer request. Cygwin users need CYGWIN=codepage:oem for the box-drawing characters, or the -z switch for plain ASCII. btedit is described as extremely powerful and should only be used under the guidance of a LifeLines developer. The README notes that gcc and clang build it with many warnings. The primary development platforms are Ubuntu 22.04 and FreeBSD 13.3. The LINES-L mailing list is the main support channel.

btedit is an administration tool used for unmangling mangled databases, and is extremely powerful. You should only use this program under the expert guidance of a LifeLines developer.

judge.reason: Its genealogy-specific report scripting turns GEDCOM family data into custom books and charts, making this more than a terminal interface for an ordinary family-tree app.

entry.title: LifeLines
entry.tldr: A 1990s terminal genealogy program with its own database and a scripting language that turns family trees into LaTeX books and PostScript charts.
entry.deeper_look:
LifeLines is a genealogy program that runs in a terminal. The main program, llines, is a curses-style interface for browsing and editing people and families. Data goes in as a GEDCOM file exported from other genealogy software, and is stored in LifeLines' own B-tree style database.

The homepage puts the draw plainly: "IMHO, the real power of lifelines is its scripting ability." Report scripts run against the database and produce ahnentafels, ancestor and descendant reports, groff and LaTeX books, and PostScript charts. llexec runs those reports non-interactively, so a family tree can feed a print pipeline.

Tom Wetmore wrote it circa 1991-1994 as a GEDCOM-driven tool. He has since released it under an MIT-style license and no longer works on it; the open source community maintains it now. That makes it a working look at how a genealogy tool was built before web apps: a data file format, a database, and a small language for asking questions of it.

The kit also ships dbverify to check a database and btedit to repair one. The project warns that btedit is only for use under the guidance of a LifeLines developer.
entry.install:
brew install lifelines
# needs a terminal with wide-character curses support; you will want a GEDCOM file to import

entry.whats_unique: A 1990s genealogy program that is still maintained, with a scripting system that builds print-quality output like LaTeX books and PostScript charts, all from inside a terminal.
entry.caveats: The original website and FTP repository are dead, the author has stepped away, recency of the latest release is unconfirmed, and you need your own GEDCOM data to get much out of it.
